steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Below is a detailed comparison of DNA and RNA, organized by key features:

1. Chemical Structure  
   • Sugar  
     – DNA contains 2′-deoxyribose (lacking a hydroxyl at the 2′ position)  
     – RNA contains ribose (with a 2′-hydroxyl group)  
     – The extra OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable  
   • Bases  
     – DNA uses Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
     – RNA uses A, Uracil (U) (instead of T), C, G  
     – Thymine has a methyl group that helps stabilize DNA’s structure  

2. Strandness and 3D Form  
   • DNA  
     – Almost always double-stranded (forming the famous double helix)  
     – Strands run antiparallel (5′→3′ vs 3′→5′) and pair via hydrogen bonds (A–T, G–C)  
     – Majority adopts B-form helix in cells  
   • RNA  
     – Typically single-stranded, but can fold back on itself to form short double-helical regions (stem-loops, hairpins)  
     – Often adopts an A-form helix when double-stranded  
     – Complex tertiary structures allow it to function as an enzyme (ribozyme), scaffold, or regulatory molecule  

3. Location in the Cell  
   • DNA  
     – Confined to the nucleus (eukaryotes), with small quantities in mitochondria and chloroplasts  
   • RNA  
     – Synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) but most function in the cytoplasm  
     – Different species are compartmentalized: mRNA exits to cytosol, rRNA assembled in nucleolus, tRNA processed in nucleus then exported  

4. Function  
   • DNA  
     – Long-term storage of genetic information  
     – Template for its own replication prior to cell division  
   • RNA  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA): delivers amino acids during protein synthesis  
     – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): core component of ribosome’s catalytic center  
     – Small RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, snRNA): regulate gene expression, mediate splicing, defend against viruses  
     – Catalytic RNAs (e.g., RNase P, self-splicing introns): perform biochemical reactions  

5. Stability and Longevity  
   • DNA  
     – Very stable under physiological conditions  
     – 2′-deoxy backbone resists hydrolysis  
     – Packaged with histones and other proteins for protection  
   • RNA  
     – Less stable; 2′-OH can attack the phosphate backbone, causing cleavage  
     – Rapid turnover suits its role in dynamic gene regulation  
     – Modified bases and secondary structures can increase stability  

6. Synthesis and Processing  
   • DNA replication  
     – Semi-conservative: each daughter duplex contains one parental strand  
     – Carried out by DNA polymerases, requires a primer, proofreading activity minimizes errors  
   • RNA transcription  
     – Performed by RNA polymerase, no primer required  
     – Yields a primary transcript (pre-mRNA in eukaryotes) that undergoes capping, polyadenylation, splicing  
     – Prokaryotic mRNAs often translated while still being transcribed  

7. Evolutionary and Viral Aspects  
   • RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life used RNA for both catalysis and information storage  
   • Many viruses use RNA (ssRNA, dsRNA) as their genetic material—some reverse-transcribing RNA viruses (retroviruses) convert RNA to DNA  

8. Summary of Key Differences  
   • Sugar: deoxyribose (DNA) vs ribose (RNA)  
   • Bases: T (DNA) vs U (RNA)  
   • Strand: double (DNA) vs mostly single (RNA)  
   • Stability: higher (DNA) vs lower (RNA)  
   • Primary role: information storage/replication (DNA) vs information transfer/expression and catalysis (RNA)  

Taken together, DNA and RNA share the basic chemistry of nucleic acids but are tailored to complementary roles—DNA as the stable archive of genetic information, RNA as the versatile interpreter and regulator of that information.
